claims.text: The proposed approach integrates high-throughput first-principles thermodynamic data with targeted in-situ melting measurements in a hybrid machine-learning model.
The hybrid model is applicable near melting across a broad compositional range of multi-principal-element and high-entropy alloys.
A neural-network or ensemble surrogate can learn mappings from elemental descriptors and composition to thermodynamic outputs.
The surrogate captures multi-element interactions and structural factors governing phase transitions.
Combining first-principles information with measured properties can produce predictive correlations that reproduce detailed experimental and thermodynamic-model results.
The hybrid approach operates at a fraction of the time and cost of DSC and full CALPHAD assessments.
Predicted melting temperatures will typically be within ±5–10% of values obtained by traditional methods.
Predicted enthalpies of fusion will typically be within ±5–10% of values obtained by traditional methods.
Predicted entropies of fusion will typically be within ±5–10% of values obtained by traditional methods.
Predicted volume changes at melting will typically be within ±5–10% of values obtained by traditional methods.
The hybrid model can accurately predict liquid-phase thermodynamic properties.
The hybrid model will achieve errors similar to traditional DSC and CALPHAD methods.
The model will provide rapid predictions over the entire HEA compositional space.
Prediction accuracy may deteriorate in composition regions represented by sparse training data.
Novel synergistic effects among elements may reduce model accuracy.
Equilibrium-based thermodynamic data do not directly capture kinetic effects near melting.
The model may inadequately represent transient, non-equilibrium melting phenomena.
The model may overfit the targeted high-fidelity training inputs.
Validation will use 10–15 held-out HEA compositions and compare predictions with DSC, calorimetry, neutron imaging, and high-temperature measurements.
The approach is falsified if more than 30% of held-out compositions have errors exceeding ±10% for key thermodynamic parameters.
